chapters.title: Chapter 1: Thoughts are Things
chapters.content: Truly, thoughts are things, and powerful things at that, when they are mixed with definiteness of purpose, persistence, and a burning desire for their translation into riches, or other material objects. A young man named Edwin C. Barnes discovered how true it is that men really think and grow rich. His discovery did not come about at one sitting. It came by degrees, starting with a burning desire to become a business associate of the great Thomas A. Edison. One of the chief characteristics of Barnes' desire was that it was definite. He wanted to work with Edison, not for him. Observe carefully the difference. The mind has a way of attracting that which we focus on most intensely.

chapters.title: Chapter 2: Desire - The Starting Point of All Achievement
chapters.content: When Edwin C. Barnes climbed off the freight train in Orange, New Jersey, he may have looked like a tramp, but his thoughts were those of a king! As he walked towards the Edison laboratory, his mind was at work. He saw himself standing in Edison's presence. He heard himself asking Mr. Edison for an opportunity to carry out the one consuming obsession of his life. That obsession was a burning desire to be a business associate of the inventor. Desire is not a hope, it is not a wish. It is a keen, pulsating desire which transcends everything else. It is definite and absolute.

chapters.title: Chapter 3: Faith - Visualization of, and Belief in Attainment of Desire
chapters.content: Faith is the head chemist of the mind. When faith is blended with the vibration of thought, the subconscious mind instantly picks up the vibration, translates it into its spiritual equivalent, and transmits it to Infinite Intelligence, as in the case of prayer. The emotions of faith, love, and sex are the most powerful of all the major positive emotions. When all three are blended, they color the vibration of thought in such a way that it instantly reaches the subconscious mind, where it is changed into its spiritual equivalent, the only form that induces a response from Infinite Intelligence.

chapters.title: Chapter 4: Auto-Suggestion - The Medium for Influencing the Subconscious Mind
chapters.content: Auto-suggestion is a term which applies to all suggestions and all self-administered stimuli which reach one's mind through the five senses. Stated in another way, auto-suggestion is self-suggestion. It is the agency of communication between that part of the mind where conscious thought takes place, and that which serves as the seat of action for the subconscious mind. Through the dominating thoughts which one permits to remain in the conscious mind, the principle of auto-suggestion voluntarily reaches the subconscious mind and influences it with these thoughts.

chapters.title: Chapter 1: Of the Division of Labour
chapters.content: The greatest improvement in the productive powers of labour, and the greater part of the skill, dexterity, and judgment with which it is anywhere directed, or applied, seem to have been the effects of the division of labour. The effects of the division of labour, in the general business of society, will be more easily understood by considering in what manner it operates in some particular manufactures. In those trifling manufactures which are destined to supply the small wants of but a few people, the whole number of workmen must necessarily be small; and those employed in every different branch of the work can often be collected into the same workhouse, and placed at once under the view of the spectator.

chapters.title: Chapter 2: Of the Principle which gives Occasion to the Division of Labour
chapters.content: This division of labour, from which so many advantages are derived, is not originally the effect of any human wisdom, which foresees and intends that general opulence to which it gives occasion. It is the necessary, though very slow and gradual, consequence of a certain propensity in human nature which has in view no such extensive utility; the propensity to truck, barter, and exchange one thing for another. Whether this propensity be one of those original principles in human nature, of which no further account can be given; or whether, as seems more probable, it be the necessary consequence of the faculties of reason and speech, it be common to all men.

chapters.title: Chapter 3: That the Division of Labour is Limited by the Extent of the Market
chapters.content: As it is the power of exchanging that gives occasion to the division of labour, so the extent of this division must always be limited by the extent of that power, or, in other words, by the extent of the market. When the market is very small, no person can have any encouragement to dedicate himself entirely to one employment, for want of the power to exchange all that surplus part of the produce of his own labour, which is over and above his own consumption, for such parts of the produce of other men's labour as he has occasion for.

chapters.title: Chapter 4: Of the Origin and Use of Money
chapters.content: When the division of labour has been once thoroughly established, it is but a very small part of a man's wants which the produce of his own labour can supply. He supplies the far greater part of them by exchanging that surplus part of the produce of his own labour, which is over and above his own consumption, for such parts of the produce of other men's labour as he has occasion for. Every man thus lives by exchanging, or becomes in some measure a merchant, and the society itself grows to be what is properly a commercial society.

chapters.title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Economic Science
chapters.content: Political Economy or Economics is a study of mankind in the ordinary business of life; it examines that part of individual and social action which is most closely connected with the attainment and with the use of the material requisites of wellbeing. Thus it is on one side a study of wealth; and on the other, and more important side, a part of the study of man. For man's character has been moulded by his every-day work, and the material resources which he thereby procures, more than by any other influence unless it be that of his religious ideals.

chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Substance of Economics
chapters.content: Economics is not a body of concrete truth, but an engine for the discovery of concrete truth. It is the study of how society manages its scarce resources. The economist must build models and frameworks to analyze the dynamic nature of markets, utility curves, and production. Value is determined by both supply and demand, interacting like the two blades of a pair of scissors. One blade cannot cut without the other, and thus cost of production and utility both play essential roles in establishing prices.

chapters.title: Chapter 3: Demand and Consumption
chapters.content: Every demand has a corresponding marginal utility. As a consumer acquires more units of a specific commodity, the utility or satisfaction derived from each additional unit decreases. This is the law of diminishing marginal utility. It underpins the downward sloping nature of the market demand curve, reflecting that a lower price is required to induce consumers to purchase larger quantities of a good.

chapters.title: Chapter 4: Elasticity of Wants
chapters.content: The elasticity of demand in a market is great or small according as the amount demanded increases much or little for a given fall in price, and diminishes much or little for a given rise in price. The general law of the elasticity of demand is that the elasticity is great for high prices, and great, or at least considerable, for medium prices, but it declines as the price falls, and gradually fades away if the fall goes so far that satiety is reached.

chapters.title: Chapter 1: The House at West Egg
chapters.content: In my younger and more vulnerable years my father gave me some advice that I've been turning over in my mind ever since. 'Whenever you feel like criticizing any one,' he told me, 'just remember that all the people in this world haven't had the advantages that you've had.' He didn't say any more, but we've always been unusually communicative in a reserved way, and I understood that he meant a great deal more than that. In consequence, I'm inclined to reserve all judgments, a habit that has opened up many curious natures to me and also made me the victim of not a few veteran bores.

chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Valley of Ashes
chapters.content: About halfway between West Egg and New York the motor road hastily joins the railroad and runs beside it for a quarter of a mile, so as to shrink away from a certain desolate area of land. This is a valley of ashes—a fantastic farm where ashes grow like wheat into ridges and hills and grotesque gardens; where ashes take the forms of houses and chimneys and rising smoke and, finally, with a transcendent effort, of men who move dimly and already crumbling through the powdery air.

chapters.title: Chapter 3: Gatsby's Midnight Gala
chapters.content: There was music from my neighbor's house through the summer nights. In his blue gardens men and girls came and went like moths among the whisperings and the champagne and the stars. At high tide in the afternoon I watched his guests diving from the tower of his raft, or taking the sun on the hot sand of his beach while his two motor-boats slit the waters of the Sound, drawing aquaplanes over cataracts of foam. On weekends his Rolls-Royce became an omnibus, bearing parties to and from the city.

chapters.title: Chapter 4: The Drive Into New York
chapters.content: On Sunday morning while church bells rang in the villages along shore, the world and its mistress returned to Gatsby's house and twinkled hilariously on his lawn. He had a yellow car, rich cream color, bright with nickel, swollen here and there in its monstrous length with triumphant hatboxes and supper-boxes and toolboxes, and terraced with a labyrinth of windshields that reflected a dozen suns. Sitting beside him, I felt a sense of wonder at the sheer magnitude of his aspirations.

soul_of_a_new_machine.title: The Soul of a New Machine
soul_of_a_new_machine.author: Tracy Kidder

chapters.title: Chapter 1: The Eagle Project Launch
chapters.content: In the basement offices of Data General, a group of young, ambitious engineers gathered under the leadership of Tom West. The task was clear but seemingly impossible: to design and build a new 32-bit superminicomputer, code-named Eagle, in record time. The competition was fierce, and digital electronics was changing at a breakneck speed. The atmosphere was charged with intense pressure, long hours, and the silent code of engineering excellence. West knew that to succeed, he had to build a team that would sign up for their own destruction in exchange for the thrill of creation.

chapters.title: Chapter 2: Designing the Microcode
chapters.content: The heart of Eagle lay in its microcode, the dense instruction sets that translated software commands into hardware actions. Carl Alsing's team of microcoders worked in a windowless room, debugging code line by line on early simulator systems. It was a tedious, brain-melting exercise of logic where a single misplaced bit could crash the entire architecture. Yet, the developers felt a strange sense of ownership. They were not just writing code; they were breathes life into silicon, shaping the very soul of a new machine.

chapters.title: Chapter 3: Debugging the Prototype
chapters.content: In the early morning hours, the first prototype of Eagle was powered on in the lab. Logic analyzers and oscilloscopes covered the benches like intensive care monitoring equipment. Smoke arose from a resistor, indicating a short circuit in the arithmetic logic unit. The engineers huddled around the schematic, tracing the copper paths. It was a race against the clock, as the company's financial future depended heavily on this machine's successful demonstration.

chapters.title: Chapter 4: The Final Integration
chapters.content: After months of non-stop work, the hardware and software layers finally began to stabilize. West stood back, watching the terminal screens show successful diagnostics runs. The system was fast, stable, and ready to meet the market demand. The engineering team collapsed in exhaustion, realizing they had achieved a miracle, creating a legacy that would outline supercomputing for the decade.

chapters.title: Chapter 1: Variation under Domestication
chapters.content: When we look to the individuals of the same variety or sub-variety of our older cultivated plants and animals, one of the first points which strikes us is, that they generally differ more from each other than do the individuals of any one species or variety in a state of nature. If we reflect on the vast diversity of the plants and animals which have been cultivated, and which have varied during all ages under the most different climates and treatment, we are driven to conclude that this great variability is due to our domestic productions having been raised under conditions of life not so uniform as, and somewhat different from, those to which the parent-species had been exposed in a state of nature.

chapters.title: Chapter 2: Variation under Nature
chapters.content: Before applying the principles arrived at in the last chapter to organic beings in a state of nature, we must briefly discuss whether these latter are subject to any variation. To treat this subject properly, a long catalogue of dry facts ought to be given; but I shall reserve these for a future work. Nor shall I here discuss the various definitions which have been given to the term species. No one definition has satisfied all naturalists; yet every naturalist knows vaguely what he means when he speaks of a species. Generally the term includes the unknown element of a distinct act of creation.

chapters.title: Chapter 3: Struggle for Existence
chapters.content: A struggle for existence inevitably follows from the high rate at which all organic beings tend to increase. Every being, which during its natural lifetime produces several eggs or seeds, must suffer destruction during some period of its life, and during some season or occasional year, otherwise, on the principle of geometrical increase, its numbers would quickly become so extraordinarily great that no country could support the product. Hence, as more individuals are produced than can possibly survive, there must in every case be a struggle for existence.

chapters.title: Chapter 4: Natural Selection
chapters.content: Natural selection acts solely by accumulating slight, successive, favorable variations; it can produce no great or sudden modifications; it can act only by short and slow steps. As new species are formed through natural selection, others will become rare and finally extinct. The relations of all organic beings to each other are highly complex, and it is this complexity that drives evolutionary adaptation over geological time scales.

chapters.title: Chapter 1: The Surprising Power of Tiny Habits
chapters.content: It is so easy to overestimate the importance of one defining moment and underestimate the value of making small improvements on a daily basis. Too often, we convince ourselves that massive success requires massive action. Whether it is losing weight, building a business, writing a book, winning a championship, or achieving any other goal, we put pressure on ourselves to make some earth-shattering improvement that everyone will talk about. Meanwhile, improving by 1 percent isn't particularly notable—sometimes it isn't even noticeable—but it can be far more meaningful, especially in the long run. The difference this tiny improvement can make over time is astounding.

chapters.title: Chapter 2: How Your Habits Shape Your Identity
chapters.content: Changing our habits is challenging for two reasons: (1) we try to change the wrong thing and (2) we try to change our habits in the wrong way. The first layer is changing your outcomes. This level is concerned with changing your results: losing weight, publishing a book, winning a championship. Most of the goals you set are associated with this level of change. The second layer is changing your process. This level is concerned with changing your habits and systems: implementing a new routine at the gym, decluttering your desk for better workflow, developing a meditation practice. Most of the habits you build are associated with this level. The third and deepest layer is changing your identity. This level is concerned with changing your beliefs: your worldview, your self-image, your judgments about yourself and others.

chapters.title: Chapter 3: The Four Laws of Behavior Change
chapters.content: The process of building a habit can be divided into four simple steps: cue, craving, response, and reward. Breaking it down into these fundamental parts can help us understand what a habit is, how it works, and how to improve it. These four steps form a neurological feedback loop—cue, craving, response, reward; cue, craving, response, reward—that ultimately allows you to create automatic habits. This cycle is known as the Habit Loop. The Four Laws of Behavior Change are a simple set of rules we can use to build better habits. They are: (1) make it obvious, (2) make it attractive, (3) make it easy, and (4) make it satisfying.

chapters.title: Chapter 4: How to Create a Good Habit
chapters.content: The First Law of Behavior Change is to make it obvious. Many people think they lack motivation when what they really lack is clarity. It is not always obvious when and where to perform a habit. To create a good habit, you must define the exact trigger location and timing. An implementation intention is a plan you make beforehand about when and where to act. The formula is: 'I will [BEHAVIOR] at [TIME] in [LOCATION].' By creating a clear implementation intention, you remove the decision-making overhead and make action automatic.

chapters.title: Chapter 1: The Challenge of the Future
chapters.content: Whenever I interview a candidate for a job, I like to ask this question: 'What important truth do very few people agree with you on?' This question sounds easy because it's straightforward. It's actually very hard to answer. It's intellectually difficult because the knowledge that everyone is taught in school is by definition agreed upon. And it's psychologically difficult because anyone who tries to answer must say something that is unpopular. Brilliant thinking is rare, but courage is in even shorter supply than genius. The future is where progress happens, and progress comes in two forms: horizontal (1 to n) and vertical (0 to 1).

chapters.title: Chapter 2: Party Like It's 1999
chapters.content: The standard view is that the 1999 tech boom was a period of collective insanity, and that the crash taught us valuable lessons about business. But the opposite is actually true. The lessons learned in the wake of the dot-com crash have become dogmas that hold back tech development today. These dogmas include: (1) make incremental advances, (2) stay lean and flexible, (3) improve on the competition, and (4) focus on product, not sales. To build a great startup, you must reject these dogmas and realize that bold plans are better than incremental ones, and a bad plan is better than no plan at all.

chapters.title: Chapter 3: All Happy Companies Are Different
chapters.content: The business version of our contrarian question is: 'What valuable company is nobody building?' This question is harder than it looks, because a company can create a lot of value without becoming valuable itself. Creating value is not enough; you also need to capture some of the value you create. To capture value, you must build a monopoly. In business, perfect competition is the opposite of monopoly. Under perfect competition, no company makes an economic profit in the long run. If you want to create and capture lasting value, look to build a creative monopoly.

chapters.title: Chapter 4: The Last Mover Advantage
chapters.content: A monopoly is only valuable if it can endure in the future. To understand whether a tech company will endure, you must look at its qualitative features. These include: proprietary technology (which must be at least 10 times better than its closest substitute), network effects, economies of scale, and branding. Additionally, you must be the last mover in your market—that is, you must make the final great development in a specific sector to capture durable monopoly profits.
